_README: AUTHORED ANSWERS FOR THE SELF-MARKED CARDS. Applied by apply-migration.mjs step 2.
38 of Hannetjie's harvested questions come from quizzes Canvas marks yourself, so no
marking schedule was ever published for them. They used to ship with the question and
a paragraph explaining that no model answer exists — which is honest about SOURCING
and useless as STUDY. It also landed on the highest-value cards in the pack: every one
of these is `verbatim`, a question Hannetjie has actually set.
The rule that produced the boilerplate was right and was applied one level too far.
Not having the marking schedule is a reason not to publish a marking schedule. It is
not a reason to withhold the answer — 'define lung compliance' has an answer whether
or not Canvas printed one. So these are written for the pack, sourced against the
Module 1 hub (which IS slide-cited) wherever it covers the ground, and the applier
appends a footer to every one of them saying exactly that. The claim the pack must
never make is that these are Hannetjie's marking points. It does not make it.
k : hash('flash|' + the question with tags stripped). NOT the full ckey, which
folds in the answer text — keying on a field this file rewrites would change
the key the moment the entry was applied. Question-only is stable and all 38
are unique under it; apply-migration.mjs asserts both.
q : a verbatim fragment of the question, checked as a substring. A human anchor
and a second guard against a hash collision.
t : the answer. HTML allowed; <b> marks the discriminator.
NO THIRD-PERSON PRONOUNS FOR THE LECTURER — apply-migration.mjs re-scans `a` and
fails the build on one. Name Hannetjie or write round it.
THREE ENTRIES FLAG A PROBLEM IN THE QUESTION rather than answering around it: the
aortic-arch fill-in calls the left common carotid a supply to 'the left side of the
heart' (it is the head), the COPD/pneumonia statement is a simplification that
emphysema breaks, and two figure questions cannot be answered without the image, so
those give the checklist the marker is looking for and say so.

answers.q: micrograph of lung tissue
answers.t:
Read the field first. This slide is a bronchiole cut across — the big pale space at the bottom — sitting in lung parenchyma, the honeycomb filling the top. Your four can come from either. The question lets you choose, and Canvas published no marking schedule, so there is no fixed number-to-name key: name the structure at the number you pick and give it a job.

1 — the bronchiole lumen. The airway itself. It conducts air to the alveoli, and its diameter is what bronchoconstriction and bronchodilation change.
3, and again at 4 — the bronchiolar epithelium. The thin band of dark nuclei at the edge of the lumen: ciliated, simple columnar grading to cuboidal, driving the mucus escalator upward. Note what the wall does not have — no cartilage and no submucosal glands — which is exactly what makes this a bronchiole and not a bronchus.
2 — a lymphoid aggregate in the airway wall. The dense purple mass of tightly packed small lymphocytes: bronchus-associated lymphoid tissue (BALT). It samples inhaled antigen and mounts a local immune response, which is why lymphoid tissue sits right against the airway.
5, 6, 8 and 9 — alveoli, the pale honeycomb filling the top of the field. Each is a thin-walled air sac, and together they are the gas exchange surface: oxygen diffuses out of them into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses back in. Any one of the four numbers answers the question, and they answer it the same way.
7 — an alveolar septum, the wall between two alveoli; that is what the long line is drawn along. The septum is where the respiratory membrane sits — type I pneumocyte, fused basement membranes and capillary endothelium, 0.5–1 µm thick — with capillaries pressed flat against it. At this magnification the dark dots strung along each septum are mostly capillary and septal cell nuclei.

Worth naming for any lung section even where this slide will not resolve them: type I pneumocytes, the flat squamous cells forming most of the alveolar wall, thin enough to diffuse across; type II pneumocytes, rounder and bulging into the sac, secreting surfactant to lower surface tension and stop the alveolus collapsing; and alveolar macrophages, free cells in the airspace that engulf dust and pathogens.
answers._why: Flagged ANSWER IS WRONG. Checked against the image itself: 1 lumen, 2 the lymphoid mass, 3 and 4 on the epithelium, 5-9 in the alveolar field - all correct. What was actually wrong is that the question says CHOOSE FOUR numbered parts and the answer only identified four of the nine, lumping 5-9 into one paragraph about alveoli in general. A reader who picked 6 or 9 got no answer to the question they had answered. Every number now has a line of its own.

answers.q: Lung Compliance
answers.t: The ease with which the lungs can expand — the distensibility of the lung tissue and of the thoracic cage around it. High compliance means the lungs inflate for little effort; low compliance means each breath costs more work. It is reduced by scar tissue or fibrosis, by a thoracic cage that has lost flexibility, and by smaller airways blocked with mucus or fluid. Lung compliance is one of the four physical factors affecting pulmonary ventilation, alongside airway resistance, alveolar surface tension and negative intrapleural pressure.

answers.q: Pneumothorax Atelectasis
answers.t: Pneumothorax is air in the pleural cavity. Atelectasis is collapse of lung tissue — alveoli that have emptied and shut. The relationship is cause and effect through the pleural seal: the intrapleural pressure is normally negative, and that is what makes the visceral and parietal pleurae cling together so the lung is pulled open with the chest wall. Let air into the pleural cavity and the negative pressure is lost, the coupling breaks, and the elastic lung recoils inwards — so a pneumothorax causes atelectasis. Not every atelectasis is a pneumothorax though: an obstructed airway or a surfactant deficiency will collapse alveoli with the pleural seal perfectly intact.

answers.q: What two misconceptions can you find in the answer below
answers.t:
The list of parts is fine and so is the purpose. The two errors are both about where the electrical activity comes from.

Misconception 1 — "the neuromuscular junctions at the SA and AV nodes". The nodes are not neuromuscular junctions. They are self-excitatory (autogenic) myocardial tissue that generates its own rhythm. A heart with every nerve cut still beats.

Misconception 2 — "electrical activity coming from the medulla oblongata via the nerves". The impulse is generated by the SA node itself, not sent down from the brain. The medulla only modifies a rhythm the heart is already producing, speeding it up or slowing it down through the sympathetic and parasympathetic supply.

answers.q: difference in normal BP (mean) in the arteries
answers.t:
Pressure falls the whole way round: arteries very high → arterioles high → capillaries low and still dropping → venae cavae lowest.

Why: blood pressure depends on the force of the heart's contraction and on peripheral resistance. Arteries take blood directly from the heart, so pressure is highest there, and their thick tunica media offers the greatest resistance to the pumping force. Pressure then falls steadily across the capillary beds — which is the point, because a capillary bed at arterial pressure would rupture — and the veins receive what is left, at low pressure.

answers.q: renin-angiotensin-aldosterone pathway and the ACE inhibitors
answers.t:
The pathway is the kidney's powerful but slow answer to low blood pressure. Renin from the kidney converts angiotensinogen (from the liver) to angiotensin I; ACE in the lungs converts that to angiotensin II. Angiotensin II then does three things: it is a powerful vasoconstrictor, so peripheral resistance rises; it triggers ADH, so water is reabsorbed; and it triggers aldosterone, so sodium — and water behind it — is reabsorbed. The last two raise blood volume, and so stroke volume.

ACE inhibitors block the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. That removes both the rise in peripheral resistance and the rise in blood volume. Since BP = SV × HR × PR, blocking two of the three factors is why they are such effective antihypertensives.

answers.q: pectinate and trabecular muscles
answers.t:
The discriminator is which chambers they are in.

Pectinate muscles are the parallel, comb-like ridges of muscle in the walls of the atria — the right atrial wall and the auricles of both atria. They let the thin-walled atrium contract with useful force and still expand to fill.

Trabeculae carneae are the irregular muscular ridges and columns lining the ventricles. They stop the ventricle walls sticking together as it empties, add strength without solid bulk, and channel blood towards the outflow. The papillary muscles arise from them.

answers.q: aortic and pulmonary semilunar valves
answers.t:
Both are semilunar valves with three pocket-like cusps, both open when the ventricle contracts and both snap shut at the start of ventricular diastole, together making the second heart sound. The differences are side, destination and pressure.

Pulmonary valve: right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk, carrying deoxygenated blood to the lungs, against low pulmonary pressure.
Aortic valve: left ventricle into the aorta, carrying oxygenated blood to the body, against much higher systemic pressure — so it is the more heavily built of the two, and it is the one that commonly stenoses. The coronary ostia sit in the aortic wall just above its cusps.

answers.q: visceral and parietal pericardium
answers.t:
They are the two layers of one continuous serous membrane, folded back on itself at the great vessels.

Parietal pericardium is the outer layer, lining the inside of the tough fibrous pericardial sac.
Visceral pericardium is the inner layer, stuck down onto the surface of the heart itself — and that layer has a second name, the epicardium.

Between them is the pericardial cavity holding pericardial fluid, so the heart slides against its sac without friction as it beats.

answers.q: Pericardium, epicardium and endocardium
answers.t:
Work outside in — and the trap is that the first two names overlap: the epicardium is part of the pericardium, not a separate structure beside it.

Pericardium — the whole sac around the heart. Hannetjie's CVS 2-3 slides name its layers superficial to deep: the tough fibrous parietal pericardium; the serous parietal pericardium lining it; the pericardial space, holding the pericardial fluid that lets the heart beat without friction; and deepest, the visceral pericardium.
Epicardium — the second name for that deepest layer, the visceral pericardium, lying directly on the heart. It is both the innermost layer of the sac and the outermost layer of the heart wall, which is why it has two names.
Endocardium — the innermost layer of the heart wall: endothelium on a thin sheet of connective tissue, lining the inside of the chambers and covering the valves, continuous with the endothelium of the great vessels.

The myocardium, the cardiac muscle that does the work, sits between epicardium and endocardium.

answers.q: tricuspid and mitral valve
answers.t:
Both are atrioventricular valves, both are anchored by chordae tendineae to papillary muscles, and both shut at the start of ventricular systole to make the first heart sound. The difference is side and cusp count.

Tricuspid — right side, between right atrium and right ventricle, three cusps.
Mitral (bicuspid) — left side, between left atrium and left ventricle, two cusps.

The memory hook is that tricuspid goes with the right side.

answers.q: semilunar and atrioventricular valves
answers.t:
Atrioventricular valves sit between atrium and ventricle — tricuspid on the right, mitral on the left. They have chordae tendineae and papillary muscles holding them, they close at the start of ventricular systole making the first sound (LUB), and they stop blood going back into the atria.

Semilunar valves sit at the ventricle exits into the great arteries — pulmonary and aortic. Three pocket-shaped cusps, no chordae (arterial back-pressure fills the pockets and seals them), closing at the start of ventricular diastole to make the second sound (DUB), and stopping blood falling back out of the arteries into the ventricles.

answers.q: papillary muscles
answers.t:
Cone-shaped muscles projecting inwards from the ventricle wall, arising from the trabeculae carneae. Each anchors the chordae tendineae, which run up to the free edges of the atrioventricular valve flaps.

Their function is to stop the valve blowing inside out. When the ventricle contracts the pressure behind the AV valve is enormous, and without the chordae held taut the flaps would prolapse back into the atrium and let blood regurgitate. The papillary muscles contract with the ventricle, keeping the tension constant so the valve stays shut in its correct plane.

answers.q: Which closure makes the LUB sound
answers.t:
LUB is the atrioventricular valves closing — tricuspid and mitral — at the start of ventricular systole. The ventricles have begun to contract, pressure inside them rises above atrial pressure, and the AV valves slam shut.

DUB is the semilunar valves closing — pulmonary and aortic — at the start of ventricular diastole. The ventricles have finished ejecting and relaxed, arterial pressure now exceeds ventricular pressure, and the semilunar cusps fill and seal.

So the two sounds bracket ventricular systole: LUB starts it, DUB ends it.

answers.q: What may cause heart murmurs
answers.t:
A murmur is the sound of turbulent blood flow where flow should be smooth. Three groups of cause:

A valve that will not open properly — stenosis. The opening is narrowed or stiffened, so blood is forced through a tight orifice at speed.
A valve that will not close properly — incompetence or regurgitation. The valve leaks and blood washes backwards through it.
An abnormal opening such as a septal defect, letting blood cross between chambers that should be separated.

Flow can also be turbulent through a normal valve simply because it is fast or thin — in anaemia, fever, pregnancy or exercise. Those are the innocent or flow murmurs.

answers.q: error in the labelling
answers.t:
The specific error depends on the figure in front of you, so work the checklist — these are where AI-generated respiratory summaries usually go wrong.

Zone boundary. The terminal bronchiole is the last conducting structure; from the respiratory bronchiole onwards it is respiratory zone. Summaries routinely put the split in the wrong place.
Cartilage. Bronchi have cartilage, bronchioles have none — they have proportionally more smooth muscle instead.
Cell types. Type I pneumocytes do gas exchange; type II make surfactant. These get swapped constantly.
Pleura. Visceral is on the lung, parietal lines the thoracic wall.
Lobes. Right lung three, left lung two plus the cardiac notch.
Airway order. Nasal cavity → pharynx → larynx → trachea → main → lobar → segmental bronchi → bronchioles → terminal → respiratory bronchioles → alveolar ducts → sacs → alveoli.

answers.q: kwashiorkor
answers.t:
It is an oncotic pressure failure. Too little dietary protein means the liver cannot make enough plasma albumin, and albumin is what holds the colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressure of the blood.

At the venular end of a capillary bed, reabsorption normally happens because oncotic pressure pulling fluid in exceeds hydrostatic pressure pushing it out. Drop the plasma protein and that inward pull collapses, so fluid filtered out at the arteriolar end is never pulled back. It accumulates in the interstitium faster than the lymphatics can drain it — oedema. In the peritoneal cavity that accumulation is ascites, and ascites is what distends the abdomen.

answers.q: hypertension and edema
answers.t:
It is a hydrostatic pressure failure — the mirror image of the low-protein case.

Fluid leaves a capillary at the arteriolar end because hydrostatic pressure pushing out beats oncotic pressure pulling in. Raise the systemic blood pressure and you raise that hydrostatic pressure, so more fluid is forced out into the interstitium at the arterial end, and less comes back at the venular end because the outward push is still elevated there too.

Filtration now exceeds reabsorption plus lymphatic drainage, and the surplus sits in the tissues as oedema.

answers.q: arteries that arise from the arch of the aorta
answers.t:
Three branches, left to right as they leave the arch:

1. Brachiocephalic trunk — the only one that divides. It splits into the right common carotid (right side of the head, neck and brain) and the right subclavian (right upper limb).
2. Left common carotid — the left side of the head, neck and brain.
3. Left subclavian — the left upper limb.

So the arch supplies the head, the neck and both arms. Note the asymmetry: the right side gets its carotid and subclavian second-hand off one trunk, the left side gets both direct from the arch.

answers.q: arteries that directly arise from the descending aorta
answers.t:
Four, with what each supplies:

Coeliac trunk — stomach, liver and spleen, via its hepatic, splenic and left gastric branches.
Superior mesenteric artery — small intestine and the first part of the large intestine.
Renal arteries, left and right — the kidneys.
Inferior mesenteric artery — the distal large intestine and rectum.

Also branching from it: the gonadal arteries to the testes or ovaries, the lumbar arteries to the body wall, and finally the split into the two common iliac arteries to the pelvis and legs.

answers.q: major blood vessels (artery and vein) in the neck
answers.t:
Arteries. The common carotid runs up each side and divides into the internal carotid (brain) and the external carotid (face, scalp and neck). Behind them the vertebral artery branches off the subclavian and climbs through the transverse foramina of the cervical vertebrae to reach the brain from below.

Veins. The internal jugular is the big one, draining the brain and the dural venous sinuses. The external jugular is more superficial and drains the scalp and face. Both end up in the subclavian vein, which joins its partner to form the brachiocephalic vein and then the superior vena cava.

answers.q: major artery to the upper limb
answers.t:
Upper limb: the subclavian artery, which becomes the axillary as it passes the first rib, then the brachial in the upper arm — the one a manual blood pressure reading listens over — and finally divides into the radial and ulnar arteries in the forearm.

Lower limb: the external iliac artery, which becomes the femoral as it passes under the inguinal ligament, then the popliteal behind the knee, and divides into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.

answers.q: veins that directly empty into the inferior vena cava
answers.t:
Four, with what each drains:

Common iliac veins — the legs and pelvis. These are the two the IVC is formed from.
Renal veins — the kidneys.
Hepatic veins — the liver, carrying away everything the liver has finished processing.
Gonadal veins — the testes or ovaries.

The suprarenal veins from the adrenal glands also drain here. Note the liver is on this list twice over in a sense: blood arrives at the liver by the hepatic portal vein and leaves it by the hepatic veins into the IVC.

answers.q: merge to form the hepatic portal vein
answers.t:
The tributaries. The superior mesenteric vein (small intestine and proximal colon) and the splenic vein (spleen — and it has already picked up the inferior mesenteric vein from the distal colon and rectum) merge behind the pancreas to form the hepatic portal vein. The gastric veins from the stomach drain into it too.

Why it matters. A portal vein is a vein with a capillary bed at both ends. Everything absorbed from the gut therefore goes to the liver first, not straight into the general circulation. That lets the liver take up and store nutrients, and detoxify drugs, alcohol and absorbed toxins, before any of it reaches the rest of the body — which is also why an oral drug dose is not the same as an injected one.

answers.q: double walled bag made of connective tissue
answers.t:
1. Visceral vs parietal. Two layers of one continuous serous membrane. Visceral is stuck to the surface of the heart itself and is also called the epicardium; parietal is the outer layer lining the inside of the fibrous sac.

2. Connected to the diaphragm. The fibrous pericardium — the tough outermost layer, anchored to the central tendon of the diaphragm.

3. Where the fluid sits. Between the parietal serous and visceral serous layers, in the pericardial cavity.

4. Function. The pericardium anchors the heart in the mediastinum, protects it, and being inelastic it prevents the heart overfilling. The fluid lubricates, so the layers slide over each other with each beat instead of rubbing.

5. "Serous". A serous membrane is a double-layered membrane that secretes a thin, watery serous fluid into the space between its layers.

answers.q: feel a pulse in an artery but not a vein
answers.t:
The pulse is a pressure wave, not the blood itself moving. Each time the left ventricle ejects, the elastic arterial wall stretches and then recoils, and that expansion travels along the arteries as a palpable wave.

A vein sits on the far side of a capillary bed. The capillary bed dissipates both the pressure and the wave — pressure has fallen from very high to low by the time blood reaches the venules, and the pulsatility has been damped out entirely. So the pumping force of the heart is simply no longer transmitted to the vein wall, and there is nothing to feel.

answers.q: abnormalities can an ECG detect
answers.t:
An ECG records the electrical activity of the heart — depolarisation and repolarisation of the myocardium — so it detects anything that disturbs that.

Rhythm — regular or irregular. An irregular rhythm is an arrhythmia, such as atrial fibrillation.
Rate — tachycardia above 100 beats/min, bradycardia below 60.
Interrupted blood flow — a STEMI is a complete occlusion, an NSTEMI a partial one.

It also shows conduction blocks and chamber enlargement. Two examples for the marks: atrial fibrillation and myocardial infarction.

answers.q: heart rate changes that occur/would occur during the different ECG readings
answers.t:
Sitting, resting — the baseline. Normal resting rate, roughly 60–100.

Supine, resting — the slowest of the four. Lying down removes gravitational pooling in the legs, so venous return and end-diastolic volume rise and stroke volume with them. Baroreceptors in the aortic arch and carotid sinus sense the resulting rise in pressure and increase parasympathetic (vagal) output, slowing the rate.

Immediately on standing — a sharp rise. Blood pools in the legs, venous return and stroke volume fall and blood pressure drops. The baroreceptors detect the drop, the cardio-acceleratory and vasomotor centres fire sympathetically, and heart rate and peripheral resistance rise to defend blood pressure. This is the orthostatic response, and the failure of it is orthostatic hypotension.

Immediately after exercise, standing — the highest. Sympathetic drive plus circulating adrenaline, plus chemoreceptors responding to raised CO₂ and lowered pH. The rate stays up through recovery while the oxygen debt is repaid.

answers.q: COPD affects mainly the conductive zone
answers.t:
The two zones do different jobs. The conducting zone — nose through to the larger bronchioles — is plumbing: it moves, warms, humidifies and cleans the air but does no gas exchange. The respiratory zone — respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveoli — is where gas exchange happens.

COPD attacks the plumbing. Chronic bronchitis inflames the airway walls and floods them with mucus, so the lumen narrows and airway resistance rises. The problem is getting air through the tubes, which is why expiration is prolonged and wheezy.

Pneumonia attacks the exchange surface. Infection fills the alveoli with exudate and pus, so the respiratory membrane thickens and diffusion across it falls. The tubes are fine; the destination is flooded.

Where the statement is loose: COPD also covers emphysema, which destroys alveolar walls and so loses respiratory-zone surface area. So the statement holds for the bronchitic half of COPD and understates the emphysematous half.

answers.q: Hyperventilation and hypoventilation can both cause blood pH abnormalities
answers.t:
Both halves are true because the same equation runs in both directions: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. CO₂ is an acid in solution, and breathing is what sets how much of it there is.

CAUSING — when breathing is the primary problem.
Hyperventilation blows off CO₂, driving the reaction left, consuming H⁺ → pH rises → respiratory alkalosis (panic attack, over-breathing).
Hypoventilation retains CO₂, driving it right, generating H⁺ → pH falls → respiratory acidosis (opioid overdose, severe asthma, head injury).

ALLEVIATING — when the primary problem is metabolic.
In metabolic acidosis (too much H⁺, e.g. ketoacidosis) chemoreceptors drive hyperventilation so CO₂ is blown off, pulling the reaction left and mopping up H⁺.
In metabolic alkalosis (too little H⁺, e.g. severe vomiting) hypoventilation retains CO₂ to generate H⁺ and pull pH back down.

So the deciding question is always which came first. The same manoeuvre is the disease when breathing is the primary event and the compensation when it is not.

answers.q: accessory muscles in forced breathing
answers.t:
Quiet breathing uses only the diaphragm and external intercostals on the way in, and nothing at all on the way out — quiet expiration is passive elastic recoil. Accessory muscles are the reserve recruited when that is not enough.

Forced inspiration adds the sternocleidomastoid and scalenes, which lift the sternum and the first two ribs, plus pectoralis minor. They enlarge the thorax further and faster than the diaphragm alone can.

Forced expiration is no longer passive at all: the internal intercostals pull the ribs down and the abdominal muscles — rectus abdominis and the obliques — contract to drive the abdominal organs up against the diaphragm, squeezing the thoracic volume down hard.

Why it matters clinically: visible accessory-muscle use — neck muscles standing out, abdominal effort — means the patient is paying an unusual amount of work for each breath. It is one of the earliest signs of respiratory distress, and it appears before the oxygen saturation falls.

answers.q: Jo is admitted to hospital with a stab wound
answers.t:
1. Type of shock. Hypovolaemic — the circulating volume itself has been lost.

2. BP = SV × HR × PR. Blood loss cuts the volume returning to the heart, so end-diastolic volume falls, so stroke volume falls. With SV down, the product falls and blood pressure with it. Heart rate and peripheral resistance rise to compensate — which is why an early hypovolaemic patient is tachycardic with cold peripheries and a still-normal BP — but once the loss outruns them, pressure drops.

3.1 Capillary pressures. With perfusion reduced, hydrostatic pressure inside the capillary falls, so less fluid is pushed out at the arteriolar end. Plasma proteins are still there, so oncotic pressure is unchanged or relatively higher. The balance therefore shifts towards reabsorption: fluid is drawn from the interstitium back into the capillaries. That is a useful compensation — it pulls interstitial fluid into the circulation to defend blood volume.

3.2 Lymph flow. Lymph is made from the interstitial fluid that filtration leaves behind. With hydrostatic pressure down, far less fluid is filtered out in the first place, and what is there is being reabsorbed instead — so there is less interstitial fluid to become lymph, and lymph flow falls.

answers.q: Left Anterior Descending coronary artery
answers.t:
1. Where its blood comes from. From the left ventricle, out through the aortic valve into the ascending aorta, then through the coronary ostia — the openings sitting in the aortic wall just above the aortic valve cusps — into the left coronary artery, which gives off the LAD (the anterior interventricular branch). The coronaries fill during diastole, when the cusps fall back and uncover the ostia.

2. What it perfuses. The anterior wall of the left ventricle; the anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum; the apex of the heart; and part of the anterior right ventricular wall. The bundle branches run inside that septum, which is what makes the next part happen.

3. Both bundle branches lost. The signal can no longer get from the AV node down to the Purkinje fibres, so this is a complete (third-degree) heart block. The ventricles fall back on a slow escape pacemaker of their own, beating independently of the atria.
Contractions: slow, and no longer coordinated with atrial contraction, so the atrial contribution to filling is lost and cardiac output falls sharply.
ECG: a widened QRS (the ventricles are depolarising slowly, cell to cell, instead of via the fast conducting system), P waves dissociated from the QRS complexes with no fixed relationship, and a slow ventricular rate — plus the ST elevation of the anterior infarct itself.

answers.q: Name two missing arteries that arise from the arch of the aorta
answers.t:
1. The brachiocephalic trunk (also called the brachiocephalic artery or innominate artery) — it divides into the right common carotid and the right subclavian, supplying the right arm and the right side of the head.
3. The left subclavian artery — the left arm.

One caution about item 2. The question describes the left common carotid as supplying "the left side of the heart". It does not — it supplies the left side of the head and neck. The heart has its own supply, the coronary arteries, which leave the ascending aorta through the ostia before the arch. Read it as a slip in the question rather than a fact to learn, but answer the blanks as asked.

answers.q: The1.Left and right
answers.t:
1. RENAL arteries — the kidneys.
2. HEPATIC artery — the liver.
3. Splenic artery — the spleen.
4. Inferior mesenteric artery — the distal large intestine and rectum.

Worth knowing for a written answer: strictly the hepatic and splenic arteries are branches of the coeliac trunk, and it is the coeliac trunk that comes directly off the abdominal aorta. The renal arteries and the inferior mesenteric really do arise from the aorta itself. Fill the blanks as the question asks, but say "via the coeliac trunk" if you are writing it out in full.

1. COMMON ILIAC veins — the legs and pelvis. These are the two veins that join to form the inferior vena cava itself.
2. HEPATIC veins — the liver.

With the gonadal, suprarenal and renal veins already given, that is the full set of direct tributaries: legs and pelvis, gonads, adrenals, kidneys, liver.

answers.q: draw diagrams of an artery and a vein
answers.t:
The three layers, both vessels, inside out.
Tunica intima — endothelium on a basement membrane. Smooth, so blood flows without clotting or friction. In a vein this layer folds inwards to form the valves.
Tunica media — smooth muscle and elastic fibres, under sympathetic control; this is the layer that vasoconstricts and vasodilates. Much thicker in an artery, and an artery also has a distinct internal elastic lamina at its inner border.
Tunica externa (adventitia) — collagen; anchors the vessel to surrounding tissue. Proportionally thicker in a vein.

What your labels must show — structural. Artery: thick tunica media, visible internal elastic lamina, small round lumen, wall holds its shape. Vein: thin wall, large and floppy lumen that collapses, valves present.

Functional. Artery: carries blood away from the heart, under high pulsatile pressure — the thick elastic media absorbs and smooths each ejection. Vein: carries blood towards the heart at low pressure, holds most of the blood volume as a reservoir, and depends on the skeletal muscle pump and its valves to move blood against gravity.

answers.q: fibrous material on the outside of the heart
answers.t:
The fibrous pericardium — the tough outermost layer of the pericardial sac, made of dense irregular connective tissue.

Three functions:
Anchors the heart in place, being fixed to the central tendon of the diaphragm below and blending with the roots of the great vessels above.
Protects the heart from physical trauma and from infection spreading in from the lungs.
Prevents overfilling — it is strong and inelastic, so the heart cannot stretch beyond a safe volume however much blood returns to it.

That inelasticity cuts both ways: it is exactly why blood or fluid collecting in the pericardial space cannot be accommodated and compresses the heart instead, which is cardiac tamponade.

answers.q: self cleaning ability is affected by smoking
answers.t:
Two mechanisms, marked separately — 1.5 for the escalator, 1 for the membrane.

Smoking and the mucociliary escalator (1.5). The conducting airways are lined with ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium and goblet cells. The mucus is sticky and traps inhaled dust, smoke particles and microbes; the cilia beat in a coordinated wave that sweeps that loaded mucus up and out of the airways towards the pharynx, where it is swallowed. That is the lung cleaning itself. Smoke damages the cilia, and the escalator stops moving. Mucus then pools in the lower airways instead of being cleared, so two things follow: trapped particles and bacteria stay in contact with the epithelium, which is why chest infections become more frequent and harder to shift; and because the cilia can no longer do the work, coughing has to replace them — the smoker's cough is the lost escalator being substituted by brute force.

Pneumonia and gaseous exchange (1). Pneumonia fills the alveoli with inflammatory exudate and fluid, which thickens the respiratory membrane. Gas exchange across that membrane is simple diffusion, and diffusion slows as the distance rises — the membrane is normally only 0.5–1 µm thick precisely because it has to be. Oxygen moving into the blood and carbon dioxide moving out both slow down. The flooded alveoli are also poorly ventilated, so the partial-pressure gradient driving the exchange falls at the same time as the distance grows: thickness and gradient are two of the three factors external respiration depends on, and pneumonia worsens both.
